nameStory: The Black-stalked Marasmius gets its name from its distinctive dark, almost black stem that contrasts sharply with its pale cap. The word 'Marasmius' comes from Greek meaning 'to wither' - a perfect description of how these tough little mushrooms can dry up completely in drought, then spring back to life when moisture returns.
description: This small, delicate mushroom is like nature's own resurrection miracle - it can completely dry out and appear dead, then bounce back to life after rain. The Black-stalked Marasmius typically measures just 1-2 inches across with a thin, pale tan to whitish cap sitting atop a remarkably dark, thread-like stem. You'll often find clusters of these tiny fungi growing together, creating miniature fairy gardens on decaying wood.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: The stem is unmistakably dark brown to nearly black, thin as a wire, and feels tough and wiry between your fingers - it won't break easily like many other small mushrooms

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small pale caps, usually tan to off-white, that feel papery when dry and become slightly sticky when wet, often developing shallow grooves radiating from the center

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White to cream-colored gills that are widely spaced and attach to the stem, giving them a spoke-like appearance under the cap

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Generally odorless or with a faint, pleasant earthy scent - nothing sharp or unpleasant

idTips.label: Resurrection Ability
idTips.description: When dry, the entire mushroom shrivels to almost nothing, but add moisture and it plumps back up within hours - try misting a dried specimen!

habitat: Look for Black-stalked Marasmius growing on well-decayed hardwood logs, stumps, and fallen branches in mixed New England forests. They particularly favor oak, maple, and beech wood that's been rotting for several years and has become soft and spongy. You'll often spot them in clusters along the same log or scattered across a debris pile in moist, shaded woodland areas.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting begins as soils warm, with small flushes appearing on logs that stayed moist through winter thaw cycles.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for fresh growth, especially after summer thunderstorms - check the same logs repeatedly as new flushes appear every few weeks.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting through autumn rains, with specimens often persisting longer due to cooler temperatures and consistent moisture.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground mushrooms disappear, but the fungus continues breaking down wood beneath snow and ice, preparing for next year's growth.

funFact: These remarkable mushrooms can lose 95% of their water content and look completely dead for months, then fully revive in just 2-3 hours when it rains - a survival trick that's earned them the nickname 'resurrection mushrooms' among mycologists.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small, pale Marasmius species, but the distinctly dark stem is your best clue - if the stem isn't dark brown to black, you're looking at a different species. Remember: 'Black-stalked' is right in the name!
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the traditional Marasmius genus to Tetrapyrgos based on genetic studies, so you may still find it listed as Marasmius nigripes in older field guides. The name change reflects our evolving understanding of fungal relationships, but the identifying features remain the same.
compareHints: As the only Tetrapyrgos species in New England, compare it with small Marasmius species in the region. Unlike other tiny white mushrooms on wood, the Black-stalked Marasmius has that signature dark stem and resurrection ability that most similar species lack. Other small wood-dwelling mushrooms typically have lighter-colored stems and don't bounce back from complete drying as dramatically.
